topics.title: Getting started
topics.summary: Take over the radio, pick a channel, talk.

sections.head: 1  Take over the radio
sections.text: This app and the stock walkie-talkie app cannot share the radio. Open Device and tap Take over: the stock app is paused and its icon hidden until you tap Hand back. The app needs Magisk root to reach the radio's serial port; allow it when Magisk asks. If taking over fails partway, the stock app is switched back on, so the phone is never left without a working radio app.

sections.head: 2  Pick a channel
sections.text: On the Intercom page the round arrows step through your channels. Or open Channels and tap a card, then Use. The first time (and whenever the list is empty when SignalDeck takes the radio) it asks whether to import your channels from the stock app; Start empty skips it and is remembered. Channels can be edited, added, backed up and restored.

sections.head: 3  Talk and listen
sections.text: Hold the large round key, or the phone's side PTT button, to talk; release it to listen. The key is amber when idle, green while the radio hears someone and red while you transmit. SignalDeck ends a transmission at the transmit limit (Device → Longest transmission, 2 minutes unless you change it); past 30 seconds the heat guard also applies (Good to know → Transmitting legally → Time limit).

sections.head: The launch screen
sections.text: When SignalDeck opens it shows its launch screen for about two and a half seconds, with the version number near the bottom, while the radio comes up behind it. Tap it to skip. Going back to the app while it is still open (launcher icon, recent apps, a notification) never shows it again; it plays only after the app was closed.

sections.head: 4  Hear more
sections.text: Turn on SOFT SQ to hear weaker stations without static, TXT to read live captions of what is said, and SCAN to search the channels of a zone for activity. Each has its own topic in this guide.

topics.title: Intercom
topics.summary: The main page: channel, talk key, activity.

sections.head: Channel
sections.text: The big number is the current channel and the title above it is its name. The round arrows step to the previous or next channel of the current zone. On NOAA weather, marine and railroad channels the talk key is dimmed: those frequencies are receive-only.

sections.head: Talkgroup
sections.text: On a DMR channel the CALL cell under the frequencies shows who you transmit to. Long-press it to pick another talkgroup without editing the channel (a plain tap does nothing, so it cannot change by accident). The list starts with the channel's programmed call, then your group contacts (Contacts page, type Group). After a pick the radio transmits group calls to that talkgroup and hears it (it is added to the receive list for the time being), the cell turns amber and reads CALL · PICKED, and the channel itself is not changed. It lasts until you change channel, scan to another one or use the VFO; pick the programmed entry to go back. Not while transmitting.

sections.head: Talk key
sections.text: Hold to transmit, release to listen. Amber: idle. Green: the radio is receiving. Red: transmitting. The phone's side PTT button and, if you switch them on in Device, the volume-up key and a custom PTT key you taught it do the same.

sections.head: Activity panel
sections.text: The panel says what is happening (ready, receiving, transmitting, who called) and lists the last events on this channel; the bars are the spectrum of what is heard, low notes on the left and high on the right (200 Hz to 3.6 kHz), and fall back to silence when nothing is heard. SignalDeck Web draws the same bars on its Intercom page. Tap the panel for Last heard. At the top, Alerts lists the warnings and refusals of the last 7 days (for example Android Auto dropping while you talk, a transmission refused on a receive-only or DMR channel, channel busy, keyword alerts), and Car and coverage lists Android Auto and coverage events. Tap one for what it means and what to do, with every line logged within 20 seconds of it, and a button to tune its channel. Below that is everyone and every channel with activity, newest first, with names from your contacts and the RadioID list, plus the recordings player and the caption transcript; tap a heard line to switch to that channel. The small cross on the panel clears its list and hides it until the next reception or transmission; the small button left in its corner brings it back at once. Last heard keeps everything.

sections.head: Activity statistics
sections.text: Last heard → Activity counts what the radio received today, in the last 7 or 30 days: receptions and minutes of audio per channel, busiest first, and a bar for each hour of the day with the busiest hour in amber. Tap a channel to tune it. Make a scan zone of the busiest puts the twelve busiest channels into a zone called Busiest channels and selects it, so SCAN searches where the activity is.

sections.head: Tone offer
sections.text: When a CTCSS tone is heard on an analog channel that has none set, the panel says so. Tap it to make that tone the channel's receive and transmit tone.

sections.head: Signal
sections.text: The classic page shows the signal strength in dBm in the yellow box. The new look shows a segmented S-meter: S1 to S9 in cyan, then amber and red above S9 (+20, +40), with the S-unit and dBm beside it. When nothing is being received the meter is dark and says NO SIGNAL, with the noise floor the radio reads beside it.

sections.head: Two looks
sections.text: Device → Radio settings → New intercom look switches between the redesigned page (the default) and the classic one. The new page's menu button and a long-press on the classic page's title switch too. Both have the same controls.

sections.head: Small screens
sections.text: On a phone whose screen is less than 700 dp tall (for example a 480 × 854 handheld), the new page is drawn smaller so everything fits above the tab bar: the channel number, its arrows and the FM/UHF/power chips move inside the readout card, text and buttons are smaller, the talk key is 132 dp and the six buttons are 66 × 44 dp in their usual places, and the tab bar is lower. It is the same page with the same controls, only smaller. Device → Radio settings → Intercom layout sets it: Automatic (the default, chosen by the screen height, which it shows), Regular or Compact. Changing it rebuilds the screen.

sections.head: Music, calls and the car
sections.text: While something is heard, the radio asks Android for the audio: music and podcasts dip under it and come back 2.5 seconds after the transmission ends. In Android Auto this is what sends the radio to the car speakers: the car plays it like a navigation prompt, turning its music down meanwhile, and the car's navigation volume sets its loudness. When Android Auto starts it takes the audio for a moment; the radio takes it back within a few seconds.

topics.title: Scanning and zones
topics.summary: SCAN searches a zone; ZONE picks one.

sections.head: Scan
sections.text: SCAN steps through the channels of the current zone, about one and a half seconds each (two and a half on phones whose radio reports a reception later, such as the Blackview Xplore 1), and stops on a channel with activity. It moves on about two and a half seconds after the activity ends. Tap SCAN again to stop.

sections.head: Skip a channel
sections.text: Long-press SCAN while it is holding on a channel to leave that channel out for the rest of this scan.

sections.head: Priority channel
sections.text: In Channels, tap a channel and Make scan priority. While scanning, that channel (even one outside the zone) is checked again after every three other channels and the scan stops there when it is busy, so you do not miss it. While the scan is held on another busy channel, it still checks the priority channel every 10 seconds (a short gap in the audio) and moves to it if it is busy. Its card shows PRIORITY; the same button clears it.

sections.head: Soft SQ while scanning
sections.text: While scanning, Soft SQ is used on every analog channel, so weak stations are caught and static is not. Each channel keeps its own Soft SQ level, set with the slider or in Channels → Edit; a channel that was never set uses 5, the middle of 1 (lenient) to 9 (strict). The level is applied on every step of the scan, not fixed when the scan starts. A channel with a receive tone (CTCSS) opens on its tone instead. Moving the slider while the scan is held on a channel changes that channel's level. A channel that only had Soft SQ for the scan returns to its own squelch when the scan stops. Turn this off in Device → Radio settings to scan with the radio's own squelch.

sections.head: Zones
sections.text: ZONE opens the zone list: tap a zone to make the arrows, the scanner and the car's channel list use only its channels, or ALL channels for every one. Each zone remembers the channel you last used in it, and choosing the zone tunes that channel (the first time, the radio stays where it is if the channel is in the zone, else it takes the zone's first channel); while you talk, scan or use the VFO the channel is left alone. Starred channels form the ★ Favourites zone; nearby-repeater imports create a zone of their own. Add a zone adds a standard channel list or a zone of your own; the ⋮ on a zone chooses its channels, renames it or deletes it (see Channels → Zones and standard lists).

topics.title: Soft SQ
topics.summary: A smarter squelch for weak signals.

sections.head: What it does
sections.text: SOFT SQ holds the radio's own squelch open and lets the app decide what you hear: the channel's CTCSS tone when it has one, otherwise a noise squelch that tells speech from static. It catches weaker stations than the radio's squelch.

sections.head: The slider
sections.text: The slider next to SOFT SQ sets how strict it is, from 1 (lenient) to 9 (strict); new channels start at 5. Each step asks a little more of the signal before the audio opens, and once open it stays open until the signal is clearly gone, so speech does not chop. The number turns green while the squelch is open and amber while it is closed. On the intercom the slider sits under SCAN and ZONE and shows only while Soft SQ is on for an FM channel; with Soft SQ off, and on DMR and M17 channels, it is hidden and the activity panel uses the space.

sections.head: Switching channels
sections.text: After a channel change the audio stays muted for under a second while the receiver settles, so you do not hear a burst of static.

sections.head: Per channel
sections.text: Soft SQ is remembered for each analog channel. With it off, the channel's own squelch level (Channels → Edit) applies.

topics.title: Live captions
topics.summary: TXT turns received speech into text.

sections.head: Captions
sections.text: TXT shows live captions of received speech in the panel. The recognizer runs inside this app (Vosk); its language model downloads once on first use, is kept across app updates, and only an uninstall removes it.

sections.head: Options
sections.text: Long-press TXT to choose the engine (on-device, or Google Cloud Speech with your own API key), the size of the on-device model, or keyword alerts.

sections.head: In the browser
sections.text: SignalDeck Web shows the live caption and the last finished sentences on its Intercom page and has a TXT key beside SCAN, MON and REC. Its Transcripts page lists every caption the phone kept (newest first, with time, channel and caller), with a search that highlights what it finds and Download .txt; below it, Caption engine chooses on the phone (Vosk) or Google (your key, saved write-only), lists the on-device models with their size and whether they are on the phone, downloads and switches models (the phone downloads them over its own connection; progress shows on the page), deletes models not in use, and shows the phone’s free space.

sections.head: Keyword alerts
sections.text: Words or phrases that, when heard, vibrate the phone and post a notification; with voice announcements on they are also spoken.

topics.title: VFO
topics.summary: Tune any frequency without a saved channel.

sections.head: Tuning
sections.text: VFO lets you set mode, receive and transmit frequency (with repeater-offset shortcuts), power, bandwidth and tones, or colour code, slot and call target for DMR, without saving a channel.

sections.head: Frequency range
sections.text: The radio tunes 136–174 MHz and 400–480 MHz only (some phones' radios tune less: see Radios that do less on the Device topic); it refuses anything else (220 MHz included) and stays where it was, so the app never sends it. If the radio does refuse a channel (for example a DMR channel without a call number), the history says so and the display goes back to the frequency the radio is really on.

sections.head: While VFO is on
sections.text: The arrows step the frequency by the step you chose and the big number reads VFO. Long-press VFO to return to your channel. Save as channel keeps a frequency you want to come back to.

sections.head: Band plan
sections.text: Under the frequencies, the VFO and the channel editor say what each one is used for: the US amateur band plan for 2 m and 70 cm (repeater inputs and outputs, simplex and calling frequencies, satellites, weak signal, APRS) and the other services in this radio's range (FRS and GMRS, MURS, marine, railroad, NOAA, land mobile, government). It turns amber with a caution where transmitting needs another licence, is not allowed or would disturb a special use. Amateur plans are the typical ARRL ones; your area's coordinator may differ.

topics.title: Record and monitor
topics.summary: REC saves audio; MON hears every DMR call.

sections.head: Record
sections.text: REC records everything received on the channel to Download/DMR/Audio. Play them from Last heard → Recordings.

sections.head: Monitor
sections.text: MON tells the radio to pass every digital call it can decode on the channel, not only those addressed to you or to the talkgroups in the channel's list. On the firmware the phone shipped with, that is the radio's own monitor mode. Receiving every call whatever its talkgroup (promiscuous receive) is not available yet: no module firmware has been proven to admit such calls on the air, so MON on a DMR channel behaves as on the firmware the phone shipped with, with every firmware. MON is for the current channel: changing channel (arrows, scan, zone, the car) switches MON off, as the radio does, and the button goes dark.

topics.title: Packet radio
topics.summary: APRS, APRS-IS, TNC, parrot, Morse, DTMF, weather alerts, SSTV.

sections.head: Mode pages
sections.text: APRS monitoring (on your region's APRS frequency), ISS APRS, the KISS TNC, SSTV receive (also ISS SSTV) and the parrot each open their own full-screen page when they start; for an ISS pass the page also shows the pass (see ISS). The top of the page shows the frequency, whether the radio is listening, receiving or transmitting, the signal and how long the mode has run. APRS: counters (packets since it started, stations, messages for you, last heard), switches for auto-ack, the digipeater, automatic beacons and APRS-IS, and three lists: Live (every packet as it arrives, and what you send), Stations (distance and direction; tap to open in maps) and Messages (tap one for you to reply), with Message, Beacon, Map, Settings and Stop. SSTV: the picture building up, its progress, the pictures received (tap one to view, share or delete it; long-press one to select several, tap the others, then Share or Delete; Done ends it; Combine with two or more receptions of the same picture selected makes a cleaner one: the ISS repeats its slides, so receptions from different passes can be lined up and averaged, which removes much of the noise of a weak pass. A sheet shows the result first: a partial picture is drawn at the bottom, so its true height is unknown and a thin, noisy strip can fool the automatic line-up (it says when it is not sure); choose a picture, move it with the arrows (long-press: 8 steps) or leave it out, Automatic goes back to the automatic line-up, and Save keeps it as a new picture beside them), Send picture, switching between 144.500 and the current channel, and Stop. Parrot: what it is doing, how many it has repeated, and Stop. The back arrow returns to the intercom and the mode keeps running; a green bar above the tabs brings its page back, and PKT always opens the packet tools with a Running now row at the top: one tap to the page of each mode that is running (several can run at once, for example an ISS pass waiting and M17 receive). The mode's icon at the top right of a page opens all the packet tools too. FT8 and M17 receive have pages of their own as well (see FT8 over FM and M17 receive; M17 is under Digital voice in the packet tools). Opening the app while a mode runs shows its page first.

sections.head: APRS
sections.text: Every analog channel is decoded passively, below the squelch too (a damaged packet fails its checksum, so noise never shows as one): positions, messages, weather and objects go to Stations and the log. While a data mode runs (APRS monitoring, SSTV, FT8, M17) its decoders hear everything the radio receives and the speaker and SignalDeck Web stay quiet; turn MON on to listen along. Monitor parks the radio on your region's APRS frequency (Device → Region: 144.390 MHz in North America, 144.800 MHz in most of Europe, Africa and the Middle East; the button names it), can acknowledge messages addressed to your callsign (off until you turn it on: tap the Auto-ack chip on the APRS page, or APRS settings → Auto-ack) and can act as a fill-in digipeater. On a radio without a 2 m band (UHF only, such as the ANYSECU W6 phones and the Atom XL) messages are never acknowledged automatically, whatever the Auto-ack setting says; the APRS page shows "No auto-ack (UHF)". Send message and Position beacon transmit from your callsign, set in APRS settings: the callsign alone in its box (letters and digits, up to six) and the SSID in its own (typing CALL-7 in the callsign box is split for you). Packets are real AX.25 frames built each time from your callsign, path and text, sent as 1200-baud AFSK: a 1.6-second steady tone while the transmitter settles, then the packet twice. To the ear every packet sounds alike, so use a decoder (another radio with APRS, or APRSdroid listening through a speaker) to check what went out. Packet, DTMF and SSTV need an analog channel; on a DMR channel they are refused. For your packets to reach aprs.fi a digipeater or iGate has to hear them on your region's APRS frequency: use high power and check the raw packets page for your callsign. While APRS monitoring, a satellite pass or another mode runs, the app keeps the phone awake (and exempts itself from battery optimisation) so timed beacons and pass tracking keep going with the screen off; automatic beacons switch the GPS on so each one carries a fresh position. The packet decoder band-passes the audio and runs five slicers side by side at different tone balances, so it also copes with radios whose audio makes 2200 Hz much louder or quieter than 1200 Hz (on direwolf’s standard noise benchmark it decodes more than direwolf itself), and it repairs a packet with a single wrong bit. APRS settings → Transmit power chooses High (default) or Low on the frequencies the app tunes itself (APRS monitoring, ISS, SSTV 144.500); messages and beacons sent from your own channel use its power. APRS settings → Packet lead-in sets what is sent before each packet while the radio’s transmit audio settles: flags (the standard AX.25 TXDELAY, default), a steady tone or silence, and its length (1.6 s by default; shorter values are for testing).

sections.head: APRS-IS
sections.text: Connects to the internet APRS network. With your passcode it gates what the radio hears, beacons your position online and delivers internet messages addressed to you; without a passcode it only receives.

sections.head: Two-way iGate
sections.text: Settings → Two-way iGate also sends internet messages out on the radio: when someone on the internet writes to a station this radio heard in the last 30 minutes (and the sender is not local too), the message goes out once as a third-party packet via WIDE1-1, and the station's answer comes back to the internet through the normal gating. It needs APRS-IS with your passcode and the radio on your region's APRS frequency (Monitor); PKT shows how many were sent.

sections.head: Automatic beacons
sections.text: Settings → Beacon: Off, Every N minutes, or SmartBeaconing, which beacons every 30 minutes when parked, more often the faster you go (every 3 minutes above 60 mph) and once more when you turn a corner, so your track looks right on the map without filling the channel. Automatic beacons, telemetry and weather reports only go out while the radio is on your region's APRS frequency (Monitor) and no TNC client owns the radio.

sections.head: Telemetry and weather
sections.text: Telemetry sends the phone's battery level, battery voltage and temperature, air pressure and the received signal as APRS telemetry; the first report and every tenth also send the names, units and scaling, so APRS sites draw graphs. Weather sends a weather report at your position with the barometer's air pressure, converted to sea level from your altitude. Both are buttons in PKT and can run every 30 minutes (Settings).

sections.head: Objects and bulletins
sections.text: Object places a marker that you own on everyone's APRS map, such as a net control point, an event or a hazard, at your position or one you type; Remove deletes it from the maps. Bulletin sends a short notice to everyone in range (BLN0 to BLN9); Bulletins lists those heard, including NWS announcements.

sections.head: Text and email gateways
sections.text: Send message → Text a phone or Send an email reaches the internet through APRS: SMSGTE texts a US or Canadian phone ("@number message"), EMAIL-2 emails an address ("address message"), 67 characters in all. It needs an iGate within reach of your signal, or APRS-IS. Replies from a phone come back as APRS messages when SMSGTE knows your callsign.

sections.head: Message groups
sections.text: Settings → Message groups: messages addressed to a group name you follow (for example CQ or ARES) notify you like a message to you, without an acknowledgement.

sections.head: Satellite passes
sections.text: PKT → Satellite passes lists, for ISS APRS, ISS SSTV, the ISS repeater, ISS voice, SO-50, PO-101 and the other FM satellites people work (AMSAT’s FM list, with frequencies and tones from SatNOGS, sorted by the next pass), the passes over you in the next 24 hours that climb above 10 degrees: when, how high, how long and where they rise and set. Orbits come from AMSAT (CelesTrak if AMSAT is down) and refresh after two days; Update orbits fetches them now. Tap a pass to track it: a minute before it rises the VFO takes the satellite's listen and talk frequencies with its access tone, corrected for Doppler (up to about 10 kHz on 70 cm) and retuned whenever the error passes 2 kHz, never while you are talking. After it sets the radio goes back to your channel. The sheet shows the satellite's direction and height and the frequencies live; Stop tracking ends it early. Higher passes are the strong ones; on SO-50 send a 74.4 Hz tone for two seconds first to switch its repeater on. Tracking an ISS APRS or ISS SSTV pass opens its page.

sections.head: Is it working?
sections.text: Under each satellite's name: AMSAT’s reports of the last 4 days from operators who listened to it (heard, telemetry only, not heard, and when it was last heard): green when people hear it, amber when only its telemetry is heard, grey when it seems off. Satellites switch off, fail or change schedules, so check this before a pass. Update orbits downloads the orbits and the FM satellite list again (it also refreshes by itself every few days); nothing about you is sent. SignalDeck Web’s Satellites page shows the same.

sections.head: VHF/UHF conditions
sections.text: PKT → VHF/UHF conditions (and SignalDeck Web’s Satellites page) answers “is it worth getting on the air beyond the usual range?”. Tropo: the next 48 hours, hour by hour, from the weather forecast’s temperature and humidity near the ground (Open-Meteo; your position is rounded to about 50 km first): grey normal, cyan slightly enhanced, green super-refraction (signals bend back toward the ground: longer range), amber ducting likely (hundreds of km). The forecast’s layers are a few hundred metres apart, so thin ducts right above the ground are underestimated; calm, clear nights after a warm day are the classic time. Aurora: NOAA’s Kp index now and forecast, and the chance of aurora overhead (NOAA’s map is downloaded whole and read on the phone). VHF aurora needs about Kp 5 at mid latitudes: point north, expect a buzzing sound. Meteor showers: the next major ones; each trail reflects 2 m for a moment, 800 to 2000 km, best before dawn. And the next satellite passes above 20°.

sections.head: ISS
sections.text: The space station's packet digipeater is on 437.825 MHz (70 cm) since ARISS moved it in 2026, and its SSTV picture events use 437.550. On 70 cm a pass shifts the signal by up to 10 kHz (Doppler), more than an FM channel tolerates, so PKT → ISS APRS and ISS SSTV do not just park on the frequency: they wait for the next pass above 10° (or the one in progress), tune a minute before the ISS rises, follow the shift every couple of seconds and come back to your channel when it sets, then wait for the next pass, until you stop. This carries on after SignalDeck restarts (an update, a reboot): it picks the ISS up again by itself. Their page shows the countdown, then the ISS's height and direction, the corrected frequency and when it sets. Fifteen minutes before a pass, orbits more than a day old are downloaded again, so a reboost of the station does not throw the pass times or the Doppler off. With Satellite passes → Record each pass on (the default), the whole pass is saved as a WAV in Download/DMR/Audio/<satellite> (about 1 MB a minute, below the squelch too), so a picture or packet that was missed can be decoded again later. Until a minute before the pass the radio stays on your channel (you can keep using it), so the top of the page says WAITING FOR THE PASS, shows the pass frequency dimmed and the time it tunes; an ISS SSTV session starts with an empty picture. ISS APRS decodes what the station digipeats; Beacon on its page (or PKT → Beacon via ISS) sends your position through it with the path ARISS, with both frequencies corrected, and only while the ISS is in view. ISS SSTV is receive only (transmitting is blocked) and saves each Robot 36 picture; during a picture the retune waits until the error reaches 5 kHz so the picture is not torn. ARISS changes the station's modes often: Satellite passes → ISS frequencies holds them (APRS, SSTV, repeater, crew voice) with a link to the ARISS status page. The ISS and satellites zone list has fixed + / plain / - channels too.

sections.head: KISS TNC
sections.text: Serves APRSdroid or YAAC on 127.0.0.1:8001 on whatever channel you are on, sending and receiving. The app sends complete frames and the radio transmits them as they come (each with the same 1.6-second settling tone first); tune an analog APRS channel first.

sections.head: DTMF
sections.text: Keys heard on any analog channel are logged. Send a sequence from the keypad or from your saved sequences; saved ones are kept in backups as DTMF.csv.

sections.head: DTMF remote control
sections.text: PKT → DTMF → Remote lets another radio control this phone: turn it on and set a PIN of 4 to 6 digits. From the other radio, key the PIN and one command digit as one sequence (a * before and # after are fine): 1 says the position (nearest town and coordinates), 2 says the status (battery, channel, signal), 3 sends an APRS position beacon, 4 and 5 turn the parrot on and off, 6 sends the Morse ID. The phone answers on the channel 1.5 seconds after the caller lets go, with your callsign in Morse after a voice reply on amateur channels. Three wrong PINs within ten minutes lock it for ten minutes, and the PIN is never written to the history or the DTMF log. It is off by default.

sections.head: Weather alerts
sections.text: NOAA SAME alerts are decoded automatically on the weather frequencies (162.400 to 162.550 MHz) and raise a notification. Where your region has no NOAA-style weather radio (Device → Region), the PKT sheet shows only a Show NOAA weather alerts button and the weather lists sit under Show all; the decoder itself still runs.

sections.head: SSTV
sections.text: Receive pictures on 144.500 MHz or on the current channel, and send a picture from your gallery. Short modes: Robot 8 BW, 12 BW and 24 Color. Long modes, marked long in the picker: Robot 36, Martin M2, Scottie S2, PD 90, Scottie S1 and Martin M1 (up to about 115 s); they fit the default 2-minute transmit limit (Device → Longest transmission), and a mode longer than the limit you set is refused with the reason. After a long transmission the phone warms up (a 120 s key raised the radio's thermal zone by about 11 °C on the bench), so the next long picture waits until that zone is back within 1 °C of where it was, about 17 minutes at most; the send button tells you how long, the history says why, and a short mode can go meanwhile. A long picture also does not start while the radio zone is already at 60 °C or the battery at 45 °C, and while it runs the phone is read every five seconds: past 70 °C on the radio zone, 48 °C on the battery, or a 2 °C climb in ten seconds, the transmission is ended early and the history says so. These sit below where the phone itself slows down; the bench used stricter numbers. Two decoders, switched on the SSTV page: Any mode recognises Robot, Martin, Scottie and PD pictures from the VIS header that starts every transmission. Robot 36 continuous works like MMSSTV: it needs no header, it locks on the line sync pulses, so a picture picked up halfway is still drawn (and moved to the bottom, where its last line belongs), it keeps the line rhythm through fades instead of losing lines, it reads each line’s colour from its separator tone, and the screen shows the static until a picture comes in. ISS SSTV always uses it (ISS events are Robot 36). Pictures, and partial ones of 16 lines or more, are saved to Download/DMR/SSTV.

sections.head: Decode a recording
sections.text: PKT → SSTV or APRS → Decode a recording (also at the bottom of the SSTV and APRS pages) finds the pictures or packets in a recording after the fact: a pass recording (Satellite passes → Record each pass), a REC recording, or one from anywhere with Upload a recording… (WAV, MP3, M4A/AAC, OGG/Opus or FLAC, any sample rate; it is kept in Download/DMR/Audio/Uploaded so it is listed next time). SSTV finds every mode SignalDeck receives from the header that starts each picture (Robot, Martin, Scottie, PD and more), plus Robot 36 pictures whose header was lost in a fade on a pass; a picture found both ways is saved once. Pictures go with the received ones, named after their mode and the time they were on the air (…_rec.png; _partial when a fade cut it short). APRS lists every packet with its time and writes the list next to the recording (.aprs.txt). It runs in the background, much faster than the recording plays (a ten-minute pass takes seconds), on its own decoders: the radio, the speaker and live reception are not touched, and nothing is sent, digipeated or gated. SignalDeck Web has the same on its SSTV page.

sections.head: RTTY and PSK31
sections.text: PKT → RTTY and PSK31 are the keyboard chat modes of fldigi and other sound-card programs, used by clubs and emergency groups. Pick RTTY 45 (45.45 baud, 170 Hz shift, Baudot) or PSK31 and Listen: the decoder finds the signal anywhere in the audio and follows it, and prints only while a clean signal is there, not static. Type a line and Send to answer on the frequency being received (or on 2125 Hz mark for RTTY and 1000 Hz for PSK31 when nothing is). Long text is split into several transmissions of about 26 seconds each. Capital letters are slower in PSK31 than small ones. On the bench firmware (FW22 or later) RTTY goes out through the module's tone generator (clean mark and space tones from the modulator); PSK31 keeps the audio path, since its phase reversals are not tones.

sections.head: Packet terminal
sections.text: PKT → Terminal connects to a packet bulletin board (BBS), node or another station's terminal on the current channel with AX.25 connected mode, the way a TNC does: enter the callsign (with its SSID, for example N0ABC-1), optionally up to two digipeaters, and Connect. Type a line and Send; what the other side sends appears below. Every transmission starts with this radio's 1.6-second settling tone, so each exchange takes a few seconds; frames that get lost are sent again, up to six tries 15 seconds apart before the link is given up. Incoming: accept lets other stations connect to you (you get a notification). It needs your callsign in APRS settings.

sections.head: Simplex repeater (parrot)
sections.text: PKT → Parrot on this channel records each transmission heard on the current channel and sends it back a second after it ends, up to 26 seconds. A station can check how it sounds, or two stations that cannot hear each other can talk through you. Very short key-ups are not repeated. On amateur channels, with your callsign set in APRS settings, the playback ends with your callsign in Morse at most once per station-ID interval (ten minutes, or your region's: Device → Region). The squelch must close on silence (a squelch level above 0, or Soft SQ), or the parrot would repeat static. It stops when you change channel; each repeat is listed in the channel history.

sections.head: Morse trainer
sections.text: PKT → Morse trainer teaches Morse code with the Koch method on the phone's speaker (nothing is transmitted). Each lesson adds one character in the usual LCWO order, starting with K and M. Play 5 groups sends five groups of five characters at the character speed with Farnsworth spacing; type what you copied and Check: at 90 % or better the next lesson opens. Set the character speed (5 to 35 WPM, 20 is a good start) and the spacing speed with the - and + buttons; your lesson and speeds are remembered. Sending practice: tap and hold the KEY for dits and dahs; after a short pause the app's Morse decoder shows what it read and your speed.

sections.head: Voice keyer
sections.text: PKT → Voice keyer holds three recorded messages (named CQ, Net preamble and My ID at first; tap a name to rename it). Record, speak, Stop: up to 25 seconds from the phone's microphone, with silence at the ends trimmed and the level evened out. Listen plays it on the phone; Send transmits it on the current analog channel after a 1.5-second lead, with your callsign in Morse after it when ID is on and the channel is an amateur one.

sections.head: ID timer
sections.text: Amateur rules ask for your callsign at intervals during a contact and at its end: every ten minutes in the US; Device → Region sets your country's interval where it is known (for example five minutes in the Netherlands), and you can change it there. Amateur channels are those inside your region's amateur bands. On them the timer starts with your first transmission after you last identified; once the interval has passed the phone vibrates and reminds you as you key (unless Morse ID after I talk does it for you). Any Morse ID restarts it; after saying your callsign, tap I just identified in the Voice keyer. PKT shows the time left.

sections.head: Morse
sections.text: Morse code heard on an analog channel, such as a repeater's identification, is decoded and written to the channel history with its tone and speed; when it contains the callsign in the channel's name it is shown as the repeater's ID, confirming you hear the repeater you programmed (5 to 40 words per minute; Settings → Morse decoder turns it off). It needs a clean keyed tone: voice, static and DTMF are ignored, and a message shows once it has ended and contains a callsign (or at least eight characters of text), so stray tones are not taken for Morse. Morse decoding pauses while packet audio (APRS and other AFSK packets) is being received and for 2 seconds after it, because packet tones through the radio can look like keyed Morse; a Morse ID sent within those 2 seconds is not decoded. Send my callsign in Morse transmits your APRS callsign on the current channel. Settings → Morse ID after I talk adds it at the end of your transmission on amateur channels (2 m, 1.25 m, 70 cm) at most every ten minutes, the identification amateur rules ask for; it goes out like the roger beep, before the radio unkeys, and is skipped when the transmission ran to within 3 seconds of the transmit limit (the radio's own timer would cut it). On the bench firmware (FW22 or later) the Morse ID goes out through the module's own tone generator instead of the phone's audio path, so it needs no 1.5 s of lead and is not shaped by the audio path's filters; on stock firmware it goes through the audio path as before.

sections.head: The PKT key
sections.text: PKT lights while APRS monitoring, SSTV receive, the TNC or the parrot is running.

topics.title: Logbook
topics.summary: Your contacts, and the stations the radio heard.

sections.head: Opening it
sections.text: PKT → Logbook. Entries are newest first; contacts are green, stations only heard are grey.

sections.head: Stations heard
sections.text: With Log heard on (the default), the radio logs stations by itself: DMR callers whose ID has a callsign in the RadioID list, every APRS station decoded, and callsigns in Morse identifications. One entry per station and mode per hour; the frequency is the channel it was heard on.

sections.head: Contacts
sections.text: Add contact starts an entry for now on the current channel, with 59 as the reports. Tap any entry to edit the callsign, frequency, mode, reports, name and notes, to mark it a contact (QSO) or only heard, or to delete it.

sections.head: Callsign lookup and grid squares
sections.text: With Look up on, callsigns heard or logged are looked up in the free HamDB directory (US and Canadian licences and some others; only the callsign is sent, and answers are kept for 30 days): the name, location and grid square fill in by themselves, and each entry shows the distance and direction from you. Look up the callsign in an entry does it on demand. The top line shows your own grid square and how many grid squares you have worked (contacts only, four-character squares, as the VUCC award counts them). Net control check-ins get their names the same way.

sections.head: ADIF
sections.text: Export ADIF writes every entry to Download/DMR/Logbook as an .adi file (ADIF 3.1) and offers to share it, for logging programs and QSL services such as LoTW or QRZ. Grid squares and locations go out as GRIDSQUARE and QTH. DMR entries are mode DIGITALVOICE, submode DMR; stations only heard carry SWL, so a logging program does not count them as contacts.

topics.title: POTA and SOTA
topics.summary: Parks and summits on the air: activate, or work the activators.

sections.head: Open it
sections.text: PKT → Logbook → POTA / SOTA (it says Activating … while you are), or SignalDeck Web’s Logbook page.

sections.head: Activate
sections.text: In a park or on a summit: Activate a park (type its reference, e.g. US-1234, or pick one of the parks within 60 km of you; POTA is asked for an area rounded to half a degree) or Activate a summit (e.g. W0C/FR-001). SignalDeck checks the reference with POTA or SOTA and shows the name. Then Log a contact for each station: callsign, reports (59 by default), their park or summit for a park-to-park contact, notes; the frequency is the one the radio is on. A station already logged on that band in the same UTC day under your activation is flagged as a duplicate. The card counts today’s contacts against what counts as an activation (POTA 10 in a UTC day, SOTA 4).

sections.head: Upload the log
sections.text: Export ADIF writes Download/DMR/Logbook/<your call>@<reference>-<UTC date>.adi (the name POTA asks for) with MY_SIG / MY_SIG_INFO and MY_POTA_REF or MY_SOTA_REF, the other station’s POTA_REF or SOTA_REF, and STATION_CALLSIGN (your callsign from the APRS settings), then offers to send it; upload it at pota.app or sotadata.org.uk. End the activation when you leave; its contacts stay in the logbook.

sections.head: Hunt
sections.text: On the air now lists the activators spotted on POTA and SOTA, the ones this radio can work first (FM on 2 m and 70 cm), then the rest (HF, CW, digital: shown dimmed). Tap one to tune the VFO to it or to log it with its park or summit. Most activations are on HF; VHF/UHF FM ones are local, so check the list now and then.

topics.title: Exam practice
topics.summary: Practise for the amateur licence exams.

sections.head: The pools
sections.text: PKT → Exam practice has the three current US question pools: Technician (Element 2, 2026–2030, 409 questions), General (Element 3, 2023–2027, 423) and Amateur Extra (Element 4, 2024–2028, 599), with their figures. They are the official NCVEC pools (public domain), in the machine-readable edition by Russ Olsen. Everything works offline.

sections.head: Practice exam
sections.text: Draws one question from each group, the way the real exam is put together: 35 questions for Technician and General (26 to pass), 50 for Extra (37 to pass). There is no feedback until the end; then you get the score, pass or not, and every miss with the right answer. Your best score is kept.

sections.head: Study and review
sections.text: Study a subelement goes through all of its questions in random order and shows the right answer after each. Missed questions brings back every question you got wrong (in an exam or in study) until you answer it right.

topics.title: Nets near you
topics.summary: Nets and get-togethers on your channels: on now, coming up, reminders.

sections.head: Opening it
sections.text: Intercom menu → Nets near you, or PKT → Nets near you. The page refreshes every minute while it is open.

sections.head: On the air near you
sections.text: Two sources. NetLogger, the program many net controls log their nets with, publishes the nets in session: SignalDeck shows the ones whose frequency is one of your channels (or whose DMR talkgroup is on one of your DMR channels), with net control, how many follow it and when it started. Tap one to tune the channel, or to see who has checked in (callsign, name and state only). And the radio itself: a long run of transmissions from several stations on one channel (20 minutes, a dozen transmissions) shows as "Sounds like a net", named when the captions catch "this is the … net". Weather and other receive-only channels are left out.

sections.head: Coming up
sections.text: Nets that come back, soonest first: the ones you added, the ones NetLogger logged on your frequencies in the last week (weekly, or daily when held on four or more days), and the ones the radio heard on the same channel at the same time on the same weekday two weeks running (or three days in a row). Tap one to tune; long-press for more.

sections.head: Adding a net
sections.text: Add a net to a channel (bottom of the page), or in the channel editor under Nets on this channel (each net is stored with its channel, so it follows the channel when it is renumbered, backed up or shared): a name, the channel, the days, the start time, how long it runs and notes such as net control or how to check in. It shows in Coming up, gets the reminder, and tapping it tunes the channel. Long-press a net you added to edit or delete it. Long-press a net found by NetLogger or by the radio and Add it as my net to keep it with your own name and days.

sections.head: Near you or not
sections.text: NetLogger gives a frequency, not a place, and many towns share one. SignalDeck keeps a net in the main lists when it is near you (a state in its name or in the logger's details is yours, the repeater's callsign is net control's, or the repeater's town is in its name) or when it is on one of your own channels and nothing points elsewhere. The rest go under Same frequency, maybe elsewhere: a net only sharing a nearby repeater's frequency, or one whose name, state or net control's call district points to another area. Long-press any net to say it is near you or not; SignalDeck remembers your answer. Your state comes from your position (Android's geocoder) and stays on the phone.

sections.head: Reminders
sections.text: Remind me: a notification 10 minutes before each net in Coming up. Tell me when a net starts: a notification when a NetLogger net opens on your channels (checked every 5 minutes). Both are off until you turn them on; tapping the notification opens this page. NetLogger is asked at most once a minute, as it requests.

sections.head: Elsewhere on the air
sections.text: The other nets in session on 2 m, 70 cm and DMR talkgroups, for interest; a DMR talkgroup net can be heard by adding its talkgroup to a DMR channel's receive list. Tap one for its check-ins.

topics.title: Message forms
topics.summary: ICS-213 and ARRL radiograms for emergency and traffic nets.

sections.head: Open it
sections.text: PKT → Message forms, or SignalDeck Web’s Messages page. New ICS-213 (the General Message: to, from, subject, date, time, message, approved by) or New radiogram (number, precedence, handling, station and place of origin, time filed, date, to, phone, text, signature; the check, the word count of the text, is filled in for you).

sections.head: Send or read
sections.text: Read on air shows the form in large type to read over a voice net. Send by APRS splits it into APRS messages to a callsign (67 characters each, one every 12 seconds; the radio must be on an analog channel and your callsign set); Send by DMR text sends it to a contact or talkgroup in 120-character texts on a DMR channel; Send by Winlink puts it in the Winlink outbox as one e-mail to callsigns or e-mail addresses (the form laid out to read, so anyone can read it, plus a code line SignalDeck uses), sent at your next Winlink connection; Save keeps it in the list. Share sends the form as text through any app.

sections.head: Receive
sections.text: When another SignalDeck sends you a form, its parts (APRS messages addressed to you, or DMR texts) are collected, or it arrives whole in a Winlink message, and, once all are in, in any order, the form appears in the list with a notification and a history line. Reply starts a new form addressed back to the sender.

topics.title: Packet finder
topics.summary: Find the BBSs, nodes and Winlink gateways around you.

sections.head: What it does
sections.text: PKT → Packet finder (or SignalDeck Web's Packet page) listens on the usual 1200-baud packet frequencies one after another and lists every packet station it hears that is not plain APRS: Winlink gateways, BBSs, nodes (their NET/ROM broadcasts and ID beacons), station IDs and beacons, and stations heard in a connection. For each: the frequency, the best signal, how often and when it was last heard, and what it said. It only listens; it never transmits.

sections.head: How long
sections.text: Nodes and BBSs identify only every 10 to 30 minutes, so a short look finds little: let it run an hour or two, or add a schedule (Scheduled operations → Packet finder, for example overnight). It stops by itself if you transmit, change the channel or a tracked satellite pass starts, and the radio goes back to its channel (or VFO) when it ends. Settings: the frequencies (in MHz; empty means the 2 m packet frequencies 144.910 to 145.090 MHz; add your area's 70 cm packet frequencies if you know them; Use my channels fills in the frequencies of your own analog channels the radio tunes, a start on a UHF-only radio such as the ANYSECU W6+, where the 2 m list does not apply), minutes on each, and hours in total.

sections.head: Using a station
sections.text: Tap a station to tune its frequency and open the packet terminal with its callsign filled in, or, for a Winlink gateway, Winlink with the gateway set. Clear the list to start a fresh search. Winlink also lists gateways on its website (winlink.org, RMS Channels).

topics.title: Pager
topics.summary: Send a POCSAG page to one RIC or several, in one transmission.

sections.head: Open it
sections.text: PKT → POCSAG page, or SignalDeck Web → Pager. The frequency starts as the channel you are on. 1200 baud is the usual speed; 512 and 2400 are there too. The function code is 3: alphanumeric text, which alphanumeric pagers display. A numeric-only pager (function 0) is not sent yet.

sections.head: Who it goes to
sections.text: Type RIC numbers, or the name or callsign of a contact that has pager RICs. Several fit in one transmission: separate them with spaces or commas. A contact with more than one RIC is paged on all of them. Your own RICs are set in PKT → APRS settings.

sections.head: Sending
sections.text: Send keys the radio at low power on that frequency. A page is about two seconds on the air: the radio fills its buffer before it keys, then the page, then a short tail. If you are not already on a low-power wide channel there, the radio tunes a low-power VFO, waits for the retune to settle, sends the page, and comes back to the channel you were on. Signing, which is on unless you tap it off, puts your callsign and a colon at the start of the text. A SignalDeck that hears it treats that as the sender and can reply; an ordinary alphanumeric pager shows it as the start of the message. The page goes through the module's symbol engine, so it sends only when the module reports bench firmware from FW21 on. On the firmware the phone shipped with, Send says so and does not key.

sections.head: Receiving
sections.text: PKT → Hear pages listens on the analog channel you are on, below the squelch, and files each page under the contact that owns its RIC. A signed page from an unknown RIC (your callsign and a colon at the start) files under that callsign. A page with neither files under the RIC number: tap it to open the thread, then Save as contact or Mute. On bench firmware the voice filter is held open. At 512 baud on this phone the audio is restored first, undoing a high-pass of about 7.5 ms that sags a long run of the same bit. The offset taken off is the average over the preamble, and during a run of the same bit the previous bit is kept until the level is a quarter of the eye past the threshold. Padding after the text is not shown. The held-path equalizer is not used at that speed. At 1200 and 2400 baud the page uses this phone's held-path equalizer and is not restored. On the firmware the phone shipped with, Hear pages says it needs the bench firmware and does not start: that receiver's audio is not something a plain slicer can read. An address word that does not check, or that needs more than one bit repaired, does not open a page, and a page is listed only when a preamble came just before it and a message word checks. A damaged address is not shown as some other number. Messages → the scan icon is monitor mode: receive only, stepping through the pager frequencies (long-press the icon to edit them) and waiting about two and a half seconds on each. It stays while a preamble is coming in, and for about a second after that so the batch can finish. A page for one of your RICs raises a notification.

topics.title: M17
topics.summary: Hear M17 digital voice, and talk back when the module firmware can send it.

sections.head: What it is
sections.text: PKT → M17 receive listens for M17, the open digital voice mode (4FSK at 4800 symbols per second, Codec 2 voice), on the channel or VFO frequency you are on, and plays what it decodes on the phone's speaker: the caller's callsign, who it is for (a callsign, a reflector module or @ALL) and their short text message are shown and go in the history and the Logbook (mode M17). Encrypted transmissions are shown but not played.

sections.head: How it works on this radio
sections.text: This radio was made for FM voice: its receiver removes everything below about 250 Hz, where M17 carries much of its signal, so an ordinary M17 demodulator decodes nothing from its audio. On the firmware the phone shipped with, SignalDeck rebuilds the missing part with an equalizer that uses the symbols it has just decoded, calibrated with test transmissions for each phone model. Measured on the Ulefone Armor 26 Ultra: 300 of 300 voice frames exact on test transmissions at the standard deviation, and a spoken test message over the air came through clearly. The ANYSECU W6+ has its own calibration: its receiver cuts the low tones harder than the Armor's, and 99 of 100 voice frames came through exact on a test transmission. The Unihertz Atom XL has its own too: its radio's sound card runs about 0.01 % fast, which the calibration and the receiver follow, and 89 of 100 voice frames came through exact on a test transmission (a little less than the Armor; the learning described below can improve it). The ANYSECU W6Plus DMR has its own as well: about 80 of 100 voice frames came through exact on a test transmission (its receive audio is noisier than the W6+'s, so more frames miss; the learning can improve this too). Other phones use the Armor's calibration until theirs is measured, and may decode less well or not at all. When the module reports a bench firmware (a version other than DMR003.UV4T.V022), SignalDeck instead asks the module to hold its voice filter open and uses a fixed equalizer measured for that phone, checked before the sync search. With either equalizer, a clean call of at least 20 frames that the error correction confirms can fit a new equalizer for this phone; it is kept only when a later call, 6 dB weaker or from another station, decodes at least as well, and the note at the bottom of the M17 page says what happened. It improves a calibration but cannot make one: on a phone whose calibration decodes nothing, there is nothing to learn from. A transmission stays one listing when it runs longer than 20 seconds, and a gap of about a second in the middle does not split it. Long-press the note at the bottom of the M17 page to go back to the shipped equalizer.  Audio the module is still muting is not searched, so a closed squelch does not become a contact. The Armor 26 Ultra has that measurement. A phone without one stays on the calibrated equalizer. The hold is sent again after you release the push-to-talk, because letting the carrier drop turns the voice filter back on.

sections.head: What it needs
sections.text: A fairly strong signal (the tests ran near -94 dBm). On the firmware the phone shipped with, M17 opens every transmission with a short preamble, which SignalDeck uses to lock on, so a transmission already in progress when you start listening is skipped until the next one. With the module's voice filter held open, SignalDeck can lock onto a transmission that is already in progress. While it decodes a transmission the radio's own sound (which would be a buzz) is held back and the decoded voice plays instead, on the speaker, in SignalDeck Web and in the spectrum; between transmissions you hear the channel as usual. On a phone whose radio drives the speaker by itself, SignalDeck cannot hold that sound back, so the buzz stays audible under the decoded voice; the M17 page says so. (The ANYSECU W6+ plays through SignalDeck, so this does not apply to it.)

sections.head: Switching to DMR
sections.text: M17 receive (and page receive) needs an analog channel, so selecting a DMR channel while it runs stops it, on every module firmware. On bench module firmware SignalDeck also gives the radio its normal DMR settings back first: M17 receive holds a filter setting there that would otherwise take the sync off your DMR transmissions.

sections.head: Talking back
sections.text: On the firmware the phone shipped with, you cannot talk back on M17: that transmitter filters out the low tones and limits the deviation, and M17 radios cannot decode what it sends (measured). When the module reports a bench firmware with the symbol engine (a version other than DMR003.UV4T.V022), Hold to talk on the M17 page sends your voice as M17 to everyone (@ALL). Your callsign is the one in APRS settings. It ends at the transmit limit (Device → Longest transmission, 2 minutes unless you change it), and past 30 seconds the heat guard applies as for voice. A short tail follows the last word so the ending is not cut off. It needs an analog channel. Stop M17 ends listening; the back arrow keeps it running with a bar on the intercom. SignalDeck Web has an M17 panel on its Packet page (start, stop, who is talking, what was heard), and browsers that are listening hear the decoded voice too.

sections.head: Text messages
sections.text: On a bench firmware, the M17 page has a message box and Send. The text goes to the channel's M17 destination, or to everyone (@ALL) when the channel has none, under your APRS callsign. It uses the same symbol transmitter as voice and takes under two seconds. Texts you send and texts you receive are listed on the M17 page and in Messages, one thread per callsign, with every text to @ALL in the shared M17 everyone thread. Each one is also a line in the intercom history. The firmware the phone shipped with can receive these texts and does not send them. If part of a text is lost, the history says the frames were lost and the text is not shown. SignalDeck Web's Packet page has the same box: who it is for, the text, and the texts sent and heard.

topics.title: FT8 over FM
topics.summary: The WSJT-X digital mode, on an FM channel, with automatic QSOs.

sections.head: What it is
sections.text: PKT → FT8 over FM runs FT8, the digital mode of WSJT-X: 15-second slots, short structured messages (calls, grid square, signal report) and contacts that run by themselves. Here it rides on the FM channel you are on, like any other audio mode, so it talks to stations sending FT8 audio on that FM channel: another SignalDeck, or WSJT-X through an FM radio. Agree on a simplex frequency with the other station; avoid the national calling frequencies. On the bench firmware (FW22 or later) the 79 tones go out through the module's tone generator instead of the audio path; the history line says so.

sections.head: What it cannot do
sections.text: This radio receives FM only, so it cannot hear normal FT8, which is sent on SSB (144.174 and 432.174 MHz, and on HF). On FM the receiver lets only the strongest transmitter through, so each slot carries one station on the channel, not dozens as on SSB, and FT8's famous weak-signal reach mostly does not carry over: FM needs a usable signal before it passes anything but noise. Expect a little more range than voice, not dramatically more.

sections.head: The screen
sections.text: The bar at the top is the slot clock: the time in the current 15 s slot and its period (1st: :00 and :30, 2nd: :15 and :45), red when you transmit in it. Under it, the waterfall of the channel's audio, 200 to 2800 Hz: the red lines mark your transmit frequency and width; tap the waterfall to move it (on FM it matters little). Then the QSO in progress and the station's state, and the list of decodes, newest first: time, signal in dB (in 2500 Hz, approximate), DT (the time offset in seconds), audio frequency and the message. CQs are green, messages to you amber. Your own transmissions are listed under Sent.

sections.head: Making contacts
sections.text: Tap a CQ in the list to answer it: the app transmits in the other period and runs the exchange the way WSJT-X does (your grid, their report, R and your report, RR73, 73), logging the contact in the Logbook (mode FT8) as soon as the reports are exchanged. Call CQ calls until someone answers, then does the same with them. Halt TX stops transmitting; if nobody answers, it stops by itself after 8 tries (RR73 after 2). Send text sends one message of your own: any standard message, or up to 13 characters of free text (A-Z, 0-9, space and + - . / ?). Your callsign comes from APRS settings. A callsign FT8 counts as non-standard (more than three letters after the digit, or an unusual prefix) can only be sent in full in a message type that has no room for a grid or report, as in WSJT-X; the history says so once when you start, and your CQ then goes out without the grid. In the reports that follow it goes as a short code the other station learned from that first message (shown as <CALL>), so a contact still completes, and a caller with such a call is answered even though its first reply carries no grid.

sections.head: Settings and clock
sections.text: FT8 settings: the grid sent with your messages (4 characters, about 100 by 200 km: empty uses the phone's location, a typed one is fixed, - sends none) and Clear list. FT8 needs both stations' clocks within about a second: the phone sets its clock from the network, and the settings show the average DT of recent decodes, which tells how far apart the clocks are. Each transmission is 14 seconds with the lead-in this radio needs. Stop FT8 ends it; the back arrow keeps it running, with a bar on the intercom to come back. SignalDeck Web has the same on its Packet page.

topics.title: Winlink e-mail
topics.summary: E-mail by radio through a Winlink gateway, or over the internet.

sections.head: What it is
sections.text: Winlink is the amateur radio e-mail system used by emergency services and travellers: your callsign is your address (CALLSIGN@winlink.org), and you can write to other callsigns or to any internet e-mail address. PKT → Winlink opens your mailbox: Inbox, Outbox (waiting for the next connection) and Sent. The same mailbox, with writing, connecting, settings, the session log and attachments, is on SignalDeck Web’s Messages page. You need an amateur licence and your callsign set in PKT → Settings.

sections.head: Please report
sections.text: Winlink in SignalDeck is new and has not yet been tested with the real Winlink system: it was tested against a test gateway over the radio and a test server over the internet, which follow the same protocol. If you use it, please tell us whether it worked (or what went wrong, with the session log): the notice at the top of the Winlink screen opens SignalDeck's issue page on GitHub.

sections.head: Detailed log
sections.text: Winlink → Settings → Detailed diagnostic log (also offered at your first connection) records, for each session, the time of every step, the protocol bytes both ways and every radio frame. Your password is never in it; the messages' data only if you tick the second box. After a session, Session log → Share log (SignalDeck Web: Download log) sends it: please do, whether it worked or not, it is how Winlink in SignalDeck gets fixed.

sections.head: Trying a real gateway
sections.text: To help confirm it works, try one session with a real gateway or over the internet and report: your phone, whether it was by radio (gateway callsign, frequency, how far) or internet; whether it connected and logged in; whether your message arrived (send one to your own e-mail address) and whether mail came back; how long it took. If anything failed, open Session log and copy it into the report (the login answer is already hidden). Start with one short message to yourself.

sections.head: Writing
sections.text: New message: To (callsigns or e-mail addresses, separated by commas), an optional Cc, a subject and plain text. Put in the outbox stores it; nothing is sent until you connect. Messages are compressed for the radio; keep them short, a page of text takes minutes on 1200-baud packet. Reply and Forward quote the original; Delete removes a message (from the outbox it will then not be sent).

sections.head: Connect: radio
sections.text: Tune the channel of a Winlink packet gateway (RMS; listed at winlink.org under RMS channels, usually 1200 baud on 2 m or 70 cm), then Connect: radio and enter its callsign (e.g. N0ABC-10), and digipeaters if you need them. SignalDeck calls it in AX.25 connected mode, sends the outbox, collects your mail and hangs up. Expect a few minutes: every transmission starts with a 1.6-second lead-in and frames lost on the air are sent again; the Packet terminal cannot be used at the same time.

sections.head: Gateways near you
sections.text: Winlink → Gateways → Open winlink.org opens Winlink's gateway list (RMS Channels) in your browser: tap RMS List, choose Packet, then CSV File (if the buttons are cut off on the phone, turn on the browser's Desktop site). Back in SignalDeck, Import the CSV opens Android's file picker, where the file you just downloaded is at the top of Recent (or in Downloads). SignalDeck Web's Messages page imports the same file from a computer. Repeat it now and then: gateways come and go. SignalDeck keeps the 1200-baud packet gateways on frequencies this radio tunes and lists them nearest first, with distance and direction from the phone's last known position (worked out on the phone, never sent). Tap one to tune its frequency and connect, to tune and listen first, or to make it your gateway. Packet finder: listen on the nearest 10 sets the packet finder to their frequencies, to check which ones you can actually hear.

sections.head: Connect: internet
sections.text: Connect: internet does the same exchange with the Winlink system (the CMS) over the phone's internet connection: handy to test your setup, or when there is no gateway in range but there is a signal.

sections.head: Account and password
sections.text: The first connection with a new callsign creates its Winlink account. Set a password for it at winlink.org, then enter it under Winlink → Settings: Winlink asks for it at every login (secure login; only a one-time answer computed from it is sent). The password is kept only in SignalDeck's private settings: never shown, logged, put in a device report, a backup or Android's cloud backup. The optional grid square is sent to the gateway when you log in.

sections.head: Session log and attachments
sections.text: Session log shows the last connection line by line (the login answer is hidden). Received attachments are listed under the message: tap one to open or share it. When new mail arrives you get a notification, and PKT shows how many are new.

topics.title: Net control
topics.summary: Run a net: check-ins, traffic and a report.

sections.head: Starting
sections.text: PKT → Net control. Name the net (the last name is remembered) and Start the net on the current channel. A clock shows how long it has run; the net keeps running if you close the sheet.

sections.head: Check-ins
sections.text: Type a callsign and Check in, or tap one of the stations heard in the last 30 minutes (DMR callers with a RadioID callsign, APRS stations, Morse IDs; names come from the logbook). Stations checking in more than 15 minutes after the start are marked Late. Tap Traffic, Late or Out on a station to flag it; stations with traffic are highlighted. Long-press a station to remove it.

sections.head: Ending
sections.text: End the net, then Share the report (name, channel, times, net control and the numbered check-ins with their flags) or Add to logbook to log every check-in as a contact. Past nets are listed under Net control; tap one for its report, long-press to delete it.

topics.title: Band scope
topics.summary: See which frequencies in a band are busy.

sections.head: Open it
sections.text: PKT → Band scope (or the PKT tools button at the top of any mode page), or SignalDeck Web → Scope. Choose a band (2 m, 2 m FM simplex, 70 cm, 70 cm FM, GMRS/FRS, marine VHF, and NOAA weather where your region has weather radio; Show all bands lists it everywhere) or Custom range (from and to in MHz and the step in kHz, anywhere inside 136–174 or 400–480 MHz, up to 1200 steps; the sheet shows how long a sweep will take) and Start.

sections.head: What it shows
sections.text: The radio steps across the band and reads the signal strength at each step. The cyan line is the latest sweep (the one in progress is drawn step by step over the previous one), the amber line the strongest seen at each frequency since Start or Clear peaks, and below it the waterfall: each row one sweep, newest at the top, from dark (noise) through cyan and green to amber and red (strong). Under the graph: the strongest signals at least 8 dB above the band's noise, with the channel name when one of your channels is there.

sections.head: How fast
sections.text: About a second a step: after every retune the radio needs 0.7 s before its signal reading is right (measured: earlier readings are 15 to 20 dB low), then the reading itself takes 0.1 to 0.5 s. So NOAA weather (7 steps) takes about 7 seconds, 2 m FM simplex (81 steps) about a minute and a half, all of 2 m in 25 kHz steps about 3 minutes and GMRS/FRS (421 steps of 12.5 kHz) about 7 minutes; a narrow custom range with only the channels you care about comes round fastest. The line under the title shows the steps, the time a sweep takes (an estimate until the first sweep is done) and the step being measured; the frequency in the strip is the one being measured now (green), and the intercom's bar shows it too. It shows activity that lasts: repeaters, nets, beacons, interference, not a single short call. On the Unihertz Atom XL a step takes about a tenth of a second: its radio settles in about 50 ms after a retune and answers a reading in a few milliseconds (measured 2026-10-30), so the same band takes about a ninth of the time, and its scanner moves on from a quiet channel after half a second instead of one and a half.

sections.head: Listen and stop
sections.text: Tap the graph (or a peak) to read a frequency, then Listen here: the scope stops and the VFO tunes there. The scope only receives; while it runs the speaker and the decoders are quiet. When it stops, the radio goes back to your channel. It stops by itself when you press Talk, for a scheduled operation and for a satellite pass, and it does not start while a pass is being tracked or begins within 15 minutes.

topics.title: Scheduled operations
topics.summary: Start something at a set time, every week or once.

sections.head: Open it
sections.text: PKT → Scheduled operations → Schedules, or SignalDeck Web → Settings → Scheduled operations. The list shows each schedule, when it runs next and a switch to turn it off; tap one to edit or delete it, Add a schedule for a new one.

sections.head: What it can do
sections.text: Listen to a channel (optionally recording it the whole time, into Download/DMR/Audio/<channel>), scan the zone, APRS monitoring on your region's APRS frequency, SSTV receive (on 144.500 or a channel you choose), send one APRS position beacon, run the packet finder, or check your Winlink mail: by radio (the gateway you last connected to, on the channel you choose; the radio goes back afterwards, and a check never holds the radio more than 20 minutes) or over the internet. The result (sent and received) goes in the history. Tick weekdays for a weekly schedule, or none for once on a date; set the start time and how many minutes it lasts.

sections.head: When it runs
sections.text: SignalDeck sets an exact Android alarm, so it starts on the minute with the screen off (it grants itself that permission with root). When the time is up, the radio goes back to the channel it was on and switches off what the schedule switched on. Only one runs at a time. A satellite pass being tracked always comes first: a schedule whose time overlaps the pass (from two minutes before it rises to a minute after it sets) is skipped and the history says so; while you are transmitting it waits up to two minutes. SignalDeck must own the radio at that time: after handing the radio back to the stock app, schedules do not run.

sections.head: Example
sections.text: Record a weekly net: Listen to a channel, the net's repeater, Record it on, Tuesday, 19:00, 60 minutes.

topics.title: Fox hunt
topics.summary: Find a hidden transmitter, or be the fox.

sections.head: Opening it
sections.text: PKT → Fox hunt, or the menu of the new intercom look → Fox hunt. Tune the fox's channel first: the hunt listens on the current channel.

sections.head: The readout
sections.text: The big number is the signal strength in dBm (higher, closer to zero, is stronger), with the S-meter and the peak since you opened it or cleared. Beeper on clicks through the phone faster and higher as the signal rises, so you can hunt without looking. Pointing shows the compass bearing of the top of the phone, corrected to true north.

sections.head: Marks and the estimate
sections.text: Hold the phone against your chest and turn slowly: your body blocks the signal from behind, so the strongest reading is when you face the fox. Point the top of the phone that way and tap Mark: the reading, your position and the bearing are saved. After two or more marks from different places, the app works out where the bearing lines cross, giving stronger readings more weight, and shows the distance and direction from you. The map shows your marks (cyan weak, amber medium, red strong; a hollow ring is a mark where the radio heard nothing) with their bearing lines and the estimate as a green ring; Plot in its corner switches to a compact plot around you, which also takes over by itself when no map tiles load (offline). Without bearings, the strongest mark is the hint. Open in maps shows the estimate in your map app. Marks are refused while you transmit (the reading would be your own signal). Marks stay until Clear marks (it asks first), even if you close the sheet.

sections.head: Prediction
sections.text: Three layers, each switched on or off under Prediction (SignalDeck remembers the choice). Bearings (on at first): each bearing line becomes a band of likely places about 15 degrees wide either side, because a compass held near the body is good to about that; with Bearings alone the estimate is the same crossing as before. Heat map (on at first): uses only how the signal strength changes from mark to mark, no bearings needed. It needs 3 or more marks at least 100 m apart, with at least 2 of them above the radio's noise floor; until then the line under the switches says what is missing. For every place on a grid around your marks (2 by 2 km with 25 m squares, made bigger when the best place sits at its edge) it asks how well a transmitter there explains your readings, with its power unknown and the signal falling off between open-ground and cluttered rates (the rate is chosen per hunt); a mark at the noise floor only says the fox is farther away than that. The map shades the likely area, cyan to red as it gets likelier, with a bright outline around the place the fox is in with 50 % probability and a faint one at 90 %. With both on, the two are combined into one estimate, which is usually better than either alone. The estimate line names the layers it used and a confidence word from the size of the 50 % outline: good (no bigger than a circle of about 100 m radius), fair (up to about 300 m), rough (bigger: usual for the heat map alone). With both off the sheet works as it did before. Honest limits: strength-based estimates are rough: walls, cars and your body change readings by 10 dB or more. Take marks in the open, spread out around the area rather than in a line, and hold the phone the same way every time. Near the fox, use Off-frequency so the readings do not all sit at the top of the scale.

sections.head: Terrain
sections.text: Terrain (off at first, because it downloads and costs battery) makes the heat map take the ground into account: for every place on the grid and every mark it looks at the ground heights in between and adds the loss a hill or ridge causes (the same model as the coverage maps), so places a strong mark could not have heard from behind a ridge drop out, and a weak mark behind a hill no longer looks farther away than it is. It works on the heat map, so it needs Heat map on. The ground heights come from the open Terrain Tiles: the first time in an area the sheet says there is no terrain for this area yet and offers Download terrain with its size (usually well under 1 MB); they are kept on the phone (shared with the coverage maps), so later hunts there work offline. The fox's antenna height changes how much a ridge hides it: tap the height button to choose on the ground (1.5 m, a handheld or a box in the grass), on a roof (10 m) or on a tower (30 m). It is worked out on 100 m blocks first and then on the 25 m squares of the likeliest blocks, and remembered between marks, so a new mark costs only its own paths. The ground model knows hills, not buildings or trees, and its heights are about 55 m apart, so a small bank or a wall does not show.

sections.head: Spin for the bearing
sections.text: Spin does the turn-and-listen for you and turns it into a bearing with its own accuracy. Tap Spin, hold the phone flat against your chest with its top pointing ahead, and turn slowly on the spot through a full circle; 20 to 40 seconds is right. The ring fills sector by sector as readings arrive (cyan weak to red strong) and the white tick shows where the phone points; the big line says Slower when you turn faster than about 45 degrees a second, Keep turning when you stop, and Keep going otherwise. After a full circle with readings all round (or when you tap Fit now) SignalDeck smooths the readings around the circle and takes the bearing at the strongest direction, or, when the weakest direction is the sharper and deeper feature (your body shadowing the fox behind you), opposite it. The result says the bearing, how far off it may be (from the difference between strongest and weakest against how much the readings scatter) and which feature it came from; the fitted curve is drawn inside the ring with the bearing as a green line. Save mark stores it as a mark with that accuracy, so the Bearings layer trusts a clean spin more than a quick point-and-mark (which counts as about 15 degrees). When the difference is too small (less than 6 dB, or not clearly above the scatter), there is a gap in the circle or too few readings, it asks you to spin again instead of storing a poor bearing: step into the open, away from cars and walls. With Fox signal set to Only the fox's, only readings from the fox's own transmissions count and the ring says Waiting for the fox in between, so the spin works best on a fox that transmits long or often. It needs the phone's compass and a position, and not while you transmit.

sections.head: Fox signal
sections.text: On a busy channel other stations change the readings too. Under Fox signal, Any signal (the start) counts every reading, as before; Only the fox's counts a reading only while the fox itself is on the air. On an analog channel the fox is picked by its tone: Fox: … offers the channel's own tone squelch, the CTCSS tone heard right now (SignalDeck decodes it from the audio; it takes about 1.5 to 3 seconds into a transmission, and this choice appears only while a tone is heard) or any CTCSS tone from the list. A DCS fox works only through the channel's own DCS squelch, because DCS cannot be read from this radio's audio, and only with Soft SQ off (Soft SQ holds the radio's squelch open; the sheet says so). On a DMR channel the fox is its DMR ID (Last caller fills in whoever was heard last) and, if you want, its colour code; leave either empty for any.
