The Diagnostics log there shows the phone's recent radio log, for troubleshooting from the computer. Web access itself, its PIN and Allow transmit from the web change only on the phone. Messages: your DMR text conversations, with quick replies and sending. Contacts: add, edit, delete and text contacts. Map: the APRS stations heard (at the positions they sent), every channel that has a location (whatever zone is selected; set one in the channel editor under Location) and, with Repeaters ticked, the repeaters near the phone (or, with Repeaters here, around the middle of the map wherever you moved it), on a dark OpenStreetMap; drag, zoom with the wheel or the buttons, click a marker for details or to tune a channel (close the card with its ×, Esc or a click on the map). Coverage: pick Signal heard or Transmit reached, then All repeaters or one repeater (or a repeater or channel card → Coverage): the measured squares, and for one repeater its terrain prediction underneath (tick Terrain prediction; it runs on the phone and appears in a few seconds, or longer when terrain has to be downloaded). The line under the toolbar says what is shown and how the prediction is calibrated; click a square for its reading. Fit zooms to the coverage while it is on. The Repeaters layer adds the repeaters within your search radius (the same catalog as Nearby repeaters on the phone); click one for its frequencies, tones or colour code and talkgroups, then Add to my channels shows what will be programmed and adds it. The Coverage choice draws the coverage maps measured by Coverage logging: signal heard (each square in the median signal, on the phone's colour scale) or transmit reached (green: a transmission from there keyed the repeater, red: no reply); click a square for its numbers. Help: this guide, searchable. A bar under the title shows any mode that is running. The phone and every open browser stay in step: a change made on either shows on the others at once.

sections.head: Decode in the browser
sections.text: The SSTV page's Decode a recording panel lists the phone's recordings (pass recordings, REC and uploads), newest first: choose SSTV pictures (every mode) or APRS packets and Decode, or Upload… a recording from the computer (WAV, MP3, M4A, OGG, FLAC, up to 200 MB), which the phone keeps and decodes at once. Progress, the stage and the packets found show in the panel; new pictures join the gallery. Stop ends it.

sections.head: SSTV pictures
sections.text: On the SSTV page, click a received picture to open it in a card on the same page: the arrows (or the ← → keys, or a swipe) step through the pictures, × or Esc closes it. Share hands the picture to the device's share menu (messages, e-mail, Facebook…); browsers only allow that on the secure address (https, port 8443). Download saves it. Delete removes it from the phone after you confirm. Select (above the pictures) lets you tick several: All, Share (all of them at once) and Delete (after a confirmation); Done ends it. The gallery shows the pictures SignalDeck saved.

sections.head: Phone panel
sections.text: The Intercom page also shows the phone itself, updated every few seconds. Battery: the level, charging or on battery (and the charger type), the current in mA (plus while it charges, minus while it drains), how fast the level moves in percent per hour over the last half hour and when it will be full or empty at that pace (it needs about five minutes after SignalDeck Web starts or the charger is plugged in or out), the temperature and the voltage. Cell: the signal in dBm and bars, the carrier and the network (2G to 5G), or no SIM / airplane mode. Wi-Fi: the signal in dBm and bars, the network name, the band and the link speed. NOT UPDATING appears when the phone stops answering.

sections.head: Transmitting
sections.text: A browser never transmits unless Allow transmit from the web is on. With it on, the PTT button keys the radio while you hold it (or hold the space bar); letting go, switching tabs or leaving the window always unkeys. On the plain address (http://…:8080) the phone's own microphone transmits. To talk with the computer's microphone open the secure address the Device card shows (https://…:8443): the browser warns once that the certificate is the phone's own (compare the fingerprint on the Device card) and asks once for the microphone; after that PTT sends your voice from the computer. SignalDeck ends it at the transmit limit (Device → Longest transmission), and the phone stops by itself if the browser goes quiet for 1.5 s or the connection drops. Only one person can talk at a time. Every transmission started from a browser is written to the channel's history with the browser's address. APRS beacons, messages and the other transmit tools follow the same switch.

sections.head: Safety
sections.text: The server only answers addresses on your own network (home Wi-Fi, hotspot) and refuses the internet. Five wrong PINs from one address wait a minute. A browser stays logged in across app restarts and phone reboots (the phone keeps only a fingerprint of each login, never the login itself). New PIN makes a new one and logs every browser out; turning Web access off closes the server. Your callsign's passcode and keys are never sent to a browser.

sections.head: If it does not open
sections.text: Phone and computer must be on the same network (a guest Wi-Fi often keeps devices apart). If the card says Not running, another app is using port 8080; restart SignalDeck. The address changes when the phone joins a different network; the card always shows the current one.

topics.title: Map
topics.summary: APRS stations, repeaters and channels around you.

sections.head: Open it
sections.text: Intercom menu → Map, or the map icon at the top of Channels.

sections.head: What is on it
sections.text: Green dots: APRS stations the radio decoded (any analog channel, APRS monitoring, ISS APRS), at their last position; APRS-IS stations are not shown. Cyan diamonds: FM repeaters; violet diamonds: DMR repeaters, within the Nearby repeaters range (15 to 120 miles). Amber pins: your channels that have a location (channel editor → Location). Blue dot: you, moving with the phone while the map is open; the soft circle around it is how accurate the fix is.

sections.head: Moving around
sections.text: Drag to move, pinch or double-tap to zoom. The buttons on the right zoom in and out, go back to your position, fit everything on screen, and (the last one) show the repeaters around the middle of the map: move the map anywhere, tap it, and the repeaters within your Nearby repeaters range of that spot replace those around you. The pills at the top hide or show each kind: APRS (the stations received), Repeaters and Channels; the number is how many there are. The map remembers which ones you turned off.

sections.head: Markers
sections.text: Tap one for a card: a station shows when it was heard, its path, speed, altitude and comment; a repeater shows its frequencies and tone and opens its details to add it as a channel; a channel can be used straight away. Every card can open the place in your maps app.

sections.head: Coverage
sections.text: The violet Coverage pill adds your measured coverage: where each repeater was heard and where your transmissions keyed it. See Coverage maps.

sections.head: Map tiles
sections.text: From OpenStreetMap (© OpenStreetMap contributors), darkened to match the app and kept on the phone for 30 days, so places you have looked at still show offline.

topics.title: Coverage maps
topics.summary: Where your repeaters really work, measured as you go.

sections.head: What it does
sections.text: With coverage logging on, the app measures each repeater wherever you hear it and checks whether it answers when you transmit. Over time the Map shows two pictures: where the repeater reaches you, and where you reach the repeater. You just use the radio normally; walks and drives fill the map in.

sections.head: Turn it on
sections.text: Device → Coverage logging, or Map → the violet Coverage pill → Log coverage (the same setting). It uses GPS while it is on, and keeps working with the screen off once you have switched it on with the app open. While it is on, the radio notification says Mapping coverage. Switch it off the same way. Everything stays on the phone. On a radio without signal readings (the ANYSECU W6+) only key-ups are recorded; the Heard layer stays empty.

sections.head: Which channels
sections.text: Channels that have a location: the repeater's position, which channels added from Nearby repeaters get automatically (or set it in the channel editor → Location). Key-ups are judged only on repeater channels, where the transmit and receive frequencies differ.

sections.head: Heard: repeater to phone
sections.text: Each time you hear the repeater, the signal strength is stored with your GPS position (only fixes better than 50 m, at most one reading every 5 seconds unless you moved 25 m). On DMR the radio reports a call only with the channel's colour code; on analog with a CTCSS tone the app checks the tone, so other stations on the frequency are not counted. The map shows 150 m squares coloured by the typical reading, from blue (barely heard, about S3) through green to red (S9+30).

sections.head: Key-ups: phone to repeater
sections.text: After each transmission of more than half a second on a repeater channel, the app reads the signal five times in the next two seconds. A repeater keeps transmitting for a moment after you let go (its tail or hang time); if that signal stands 8 dB above the channel's quiet noise floor, you keyed it from there (green). If nothing comes back it is a no reply (red). The Last heard history notes each result.

sections.head: Driving with a steady signal
sections.text: While a station keeps transmitting, a reading is stored every 2 seconds as long as you keep moving (every 5 seconds when you stand still), so a drive draws a continuous track: at 60 mph about one reading every 55 m.

sections.head: NOAA weather: the best way to start
sections.text: NOAA Weather Radio channels (162.400 to 162.550 MHz) transmit all the time, so on them every reading is stored, heard or not: weak spots and dead zones show up in blue instead of staying empty. Give the NOAA channel its transmitter's location (channel editor → Location), select it, turn on logging and drive around: the map shows that transmitter's real coverage, and the prediction calibrates itself from it.

sections.head: On the Unihertz Atom XL
sections.text: Coverage logging reads the signal during receptions, because that is what it maps. On this phone, whose radio sits behind a USB bridge chip, readings during a reception may cut its audio for a few seconds (SignalDeck restarts the bridge by itself); the stored readings are not affected.

sections.head: While scanning
sections.text: Logging carries on during a scan: whenever the scan stops on a channel that has a location and hears it, the readings are stored for that repeater. Each channel keeps its own quiet noise floor across scan visits, so a transmission after the scan stops on a repeater is judged too.

sections.head: Key-up test
sections.text: Coverage sheet → Key-up test here: on an FM repeater channel it transmits your callsign in Morse (about 3 seconds at 20 words per minute, your station identification) and records whether the repeater answered, without having to call anyone. It needs your callsign (PKT → APRS settings) and logging on, and asks before transmitting. On DMR, call the Parrot (private call 9990 on BrandMeister) instead: hearing your own call back proves both directions. Use it sparingly; repeaters are shared.

sections.head: Reading the two layers
sections.text: The Heard layer usually reaches further than Key-ups: the repeater has a big antenna and more power than a handheld. Plan by Key-ups. No-reply squares are shown only for repeaters that have answered you somewhere, since a repeater with no tail never answers. Someone else talking right after you can look like a key-up; it is rare.

sections.head: Live while you watch
sections.text: With the map open, new readings appear within a couple of seconds and your blue dot follows you. The prediction re-calibrates itself from the new readings at most every 2 minutes (a full recalculation takes about half a minute).

sections.head: Focus and details
sections.text: The Coverage sheet picks the layer (Off, Heard, Key-ups) and one repeater or all of them (each square then shows the best one). Tap a square for its reading, or a channel pin → Coverage to focus on it. The legend in the corner opens the sheet.

sections.head: Terrain prediction
sections.text: Pick one repeater (Coverage sheet, or a repeater or channel on the map → Coverage) and the map adds faint squares: the range predicted from the hills and valleys between you and the repeater, by default (Auto) as far as the transmitter's power and antenna height can carry over flat ground, up to 50 miles, or a range you pick. It works before you have measured anything, so you can check a repeater before adding it. A picked range is a minimum: the prediction always reaches out to your position and to everything you have measured (up to 50 miles), so a reception far outside the expected range is never left off the map. The repeater's antenna height is Auto by default: once your Heard readings cover a range of distances, the app tries heights from 10 to 350 m and keeps the one that explains them best (a tall tower carries much further over the hills); with fewer readings it uses 30 m. Pick a height, or Set the exact one, if you know it. Transmitter power works the same way: Unknown assumes 50 W and lets your measurements correct the level; NOAA Weather Radio stations publish theirs (most are 1000 W), and repeater owners often list theirs.

sections.head: How it is calculated
sections.text: For each square: the loss over smooth ground (the direct signal plus its reflection off the ground within the radio horizon, the earth's curve beyond it, per ITU-R P.526), plus whatever the hills between add as obstacles. Heights are taken above the surrounding ground, so a transmitter on a hill or a phone on a rise gets credit, and a valley costs signal. The transmitter's power and antenna height set the level; your measurements correct it.

sections.head: How the prediction learns
sections.text: It starts from typical numbers (a 50 W repeater, a 4 W handheld, 12 dB for trees, buildings and your body). Your Heard readings shift its signal level to match what you really received; your key-ups move the limit of where you can reach the repeater. Until you have key-ups, the reach follows the Heard correction too, since it is the same path both ways. Each square's card says whether it is measured or predicted and how well calibrated the prediction is. Your altitude counts through the terrain: the ground height at your position and at the repeater is in every calculation, so a hilltop or a valley is accounted for (the phone's own GPS altitude is not used: it is typically 10 to 30 m off). Trees and buildings are not in the terrain data, so forests and towns usually come out weaker than predicted until you have measured there.

sections.head: In the browser
sections.text: SignalDeck Web’s Map shows the same layers: the measured squares for all repeaters or one, and the terrain prediction for one repeater (the same settings as here: antenna height, power and range from the Coverage sheet).

sections.head: Terrain data
sections.text: Heights come from the open Terrain Tiles (AWS Open Data, about 55 m detail). The first prediction for an area downloads them (a few megabytes); after that they are kept on the phone and predictions work offline.

sections.head: Export and clear
sections.text: Export writes Download/DMR/Coverage/<date>/ with coverage_rx.csv and coverage_tx.csv (every reading, for a spreadsheet) and coverage.kml, which opens in Google Earth with coloured squares and green/red key-up points per repeater. Clear deletes the readings of the selected repeater, or all of them.

sections.head: Good habits
sections.text: Carry the phone the same way when you compare places: a pocket or a car costs 10 to 20 dB. Do not key a repeater just to test it; use your normal conversations, and identify with your callsign as always.

topics.title: Android Auto
topics.summary: The radio on your car's screen.

sections.head: In the car
sections.text: Connect the phone to Android Auto and the radio appears among the media apps (SignalDeck): on the car's app list (it may be on a later page) and as the media card on the car's home screen; tap the card for the full media screen. Press play there (or on the card) to hear the radio through the car's speakers: the radio then becomes the car's media source, like any music app, and pause hands the speakers back. Its card and media screen show a small version of the intercom panel: the zone (when the channel is in it), the channel digits (red while you transmit), frequency, mode chips, a state badge (receiving, transmitting, scanning, ready, paused) and a live signal meter. During a DMR call the chips become the talker's callsign and the talkgroup (or Private call), and the subtitle reads who is talking with their DMR ID and the talkgroup (for example N0CALL Demo Operator · 9999999 · TG 91); Radio controls shows the same on its Talking line; the channel list shows each channel's number tile. The radio keeps its connection to the radio module on the phone; Android Auto only shows and controls it.

sections.head: Choosing a channel
sections.text: On the media screen, the arrow at the top left opens the channel list: Last heard first (who and what was received, newest first; tap one to tune that channel), then a tab for each zone (including Favourites once you have starred channels), with More holding the rest and All channels. Tap a channel to tune it. In Radio controls the Channels button lists the same. Previous and next, also on the steering wheel, step through the zone. The search button finds a channel by name, number or frequency, and "Hey Google, play NOAA WX6 on SignalDeck" works too.

sections.head: Talk
sections.text: The microphone button on the media screen transmits: tap to start, tap again to stop; it ends by itself at the transmit limit (Device → Longest transmission, 2 minutes unless you change it). Receive-only channels refuse it. With Device → Car microphone in Android Auto on (the default) and the car connected over Bluetooth too, the car's own microphone is used through its hands-free link (the link takes a second to come up before the radio keys); otherwise the phone's microphone. The phone's side PTT key works as always.

sections.head: Radio controls (big Talk button)
sections.text: Android Auto gives media apps only small buttons, so the radio also has its own car screen. It is off by default: turn on Device → Full-screen Radio controls in the car, then reconnect the car, and open Radio controls from the car's app list. It shows the live panel, the channel and its status, two wide buttons, TALK (green; red with STOP TALKING while you transmit) and Channels, and arrows at the top right for the previous and next channel. Channels lists Favourites first (your starred channels; until you star some it says how), then every zone and All channels; tap a channel to tune it. Inside a zone, Scan at the top scans exactly that zone (Stop scan ends it). While it is on, Android Auto lists it instead of the media app; the radio's media card, steering-wheel buttons and lock-screen controls still work. If the car does not list it, see If the radio is missing. The radio history records what Android Auto did (connected, opened the media app or Radio controls, took the sound away), so a drive can be checked afterwards. Talk works as on the media screen, with the car microphone when available.

sections.head: Scan, pause
sections.text: The scan button starts and stops a scan of the zone. Pause mutes the radio's sound; it keeps receiving, decoding and logging underneath, and play brings the sound back. Pressing play in the car makes the radio the car's media source (other media pauses).

sections.head: How it sounds
sections.text: When you are not playing the radio as the car's media, anything it receives still comes through the car speakers like a navigation prompt, with the car's music turned down meanwhile; the navigation volume sets its loudness.

sections.head: Messages read aloud
sections.text: Incoming DMR texts, APRS messages (over the air and APRS-IS) and NOAA weather alerts arrive as conversations: on the phone, and in the car Android Auto announces them and reads them aloud. Reply by voice and the answer goes back the way the message came: a DMR text to that ID or talkgroup (needs a DMR channel tuned), an APRS message over APRS-IS when it came from there, otherwise over the air on the current channel. Weather alerts have no reply. Diagnostics → Post a test car message shows what it looks like (its reply is never sent).

sections.head: Coverage while you drive
sections.text: With Device → Log coverage in the car on (the default), coverage logging starts when Android Auto connects and stops when it disconnects (unless you had switched it on yourself), so drives fill in the coverage maps by themselves.

sections.head: Next as a talk key
sections.text: Device → Steering-wheel Next talks (tap to choose Off, Hold or Double-press; Double-press by default, only while Android Auto is connected). Hold: hold the wheel's Next button for half a second and the radio transmits until you let go; some cars send the release late or not at all, so if it keeps transmitting, press Next once more to stop. A short press still goes to the next channel. Double-press: press Next twice quickly to transmit and once to stop; a single press goes to the next channel after half a second. Double-press uses only presses, so it works even where releases are unreliable. Both need the car to pass the button itself to the app: some cars send Next only as a command, and the history then says so. Steering-wheel microphone chooses the microphone for transmissions started from the wheel. Car (as a call, the default): the car's microphone works through its hands-free link, and while that link is open the car treats the wheel as call controls, so a wheel start becomes a short "call" (SignalDeck: talking) and the wheel's hang-up button or End on the car screen stops the transmission; it never appears in the call log. If the car does not open its microphone within 4 seconds, that transmission uses the phone's microphone and the history says so. Phone: the phone's microphone, and the wheel's Next or play/pause stops as usual. Stop when I stop talking (Off, 1.5, 2.5 or 4 s; 1.5 s by default): for wheel-started transmissions, the radio unkeys once you have been quiet that long (or after 6 seconds if you never speak), measured against the road noise. With a mode on, the history also shows the first wheel presses of each drive.

sections.head: Steering-wheel Talk
sections.text: Device → Steering-wheel play/pause talks (off by default): in Android Auto the wheel's play/pause button starts transmitting and a second press stops (the transmit limit as always). The play/pause button on the car screen still pauses the radio's sound. Only the wheel's media buttons reach an app (play/pause, previous, next): the voice button belongs to Google's assistant (it needs the Google app enabled on the phone; "Voice commands are not available right now" means it is not) and the phone button to the car's dialer.

sections.head: Last heard
sections.text: In Radio controls → Channels, Last heard lists who and what was received, newest first, with the time and channel (and talkgroup for DMR). Tap one to tune that channel.

sections.head: If Android Auto drops while you talk
sections.text: With the phone on a USB cable, the radio's own transmission can get into the cable and reset the phone's USB port: Android Auto disconnects about a second after you start talking and reconnects when you stop, and the phone stops charging meanwhile. It does not matter which Talk button you use. It depends on the frequency, not on where the antenna is (the cable itself picks up the signal): in one car a 2 m repeater transmitting on 144.770 MHz at high power dropped it every time while 146.370 MHz did not. The app notices it: the radio history notes the channel and frequency and the phone shows a notification. What helps: a snap-on ferrite choke on the cable close to the phone, a shorter, better-shielded cable, Low power for that channel (Channels → edit the channel), or wireless Android Auto if the car has it.

sections.head: If the radio is missing
sections.text: Android Auto only trusts apps installed from the Play Store. For this app it plays the sound and the steering-wheel buttons work, but SignalDeck (and Radio controls) is missing from the car's app list, and tapping its card on the car's home screen opens the app on the phone instead of the car's media screen. The app checks this setting (with root): while it is off, the Device page shows Android Auto is hiding this app (tap it for the steps and a button that opens Android Auto's settings), and when the car connects the phone gets a notification and the radio history notes it. To fix it, allow Unknown sources once: on the phone open Android Auto's settings, tap the version number at the bottom ten times to unlock the developer settings, then in the ⋮ menu choose Developer settings and turn on Unknown sources. Disconnect and reconnect the car. Android Auto's desktop test head unit does not check this, so the radio appears there either way. Once, with Unknown sources already on, Android Auto connected without loading the radio at all (same symptoms); unplugging the cable and plugging it in again fixed it. The app notices this too: if Android Auto has not loaded the radio 30 seconds after connecting, the radio history and a notification say to reconnect.

topics.title: Widget and notification
topics.summary: Control the radio without opening the app.

sections.head: Notification
sections.text: While the radio is on, its notification shows the channel, frequency and what is happening (ready, receiving, transmitting, scanning) with three buttons: previous channel, scan or stop scan, next channel. Tap the notification to open the app.

sections.head: Home-screen widget
sections.text: Device → Home widget asks the home screen to add it (confirm with Add), or long-press the home screen, choose Widgets, find SignalDeck and drag the Radio widget out. It can be resized. It shows the channel number and name and the same status line, with previous, scan, next and Talk buttons. Tap the channel to open the app.

sections.head: Talk from the widget
sections.text: A widget cannot feel a held finger, so Talk works tap to start, tap to stop: the button turns red while you transmit. Transmitting stops by itself at the transmit limit (Device → Longest transmission, 2 minutes unless you change it). Receive-only channels refuse it.

sections.head: When the radio is off
sections.text: The buttons need the app to own the radio. If it does not, they say so; tap the channel to open the app.

topics.title: Emergency and roger beep
topics.summary: Send your position; an end-of-talk tone.

sections.head: Emergency
sections.text: Intercom menu → Emergency, or Device → Emergency. It sends on the channel you are on. On a DMR channel: a text 'EMERGENCY <message> @ latitude,longitude +-accuracy' to the contact or talkgroup you choose in the sheet (it is remembered). On an analog channel: an APRS position with the emergency symbol and 'EMERGENCY <message>' as the comment, or an EMERGENCY status report when the phone has no position fix; this needs your callsign in PKT → APRS settings.

sections.head: Hold to send
sections.text: The red key must be held for two seconds, so a stray tap never sends. Lifting early cancels. Afterwards the sheet says what was sent; hold again to repeat it.

sections.head: Pick the right channel
sections.text: Switch to the channel where someone will hear you first: your repeater or talkgroup for DMR, the local APRS frequency (Device → Region shows yours) for APRS. Only use it for a real emergency.

sections.head: Roger beep
sections.text: Device → Roger beep: Off, Beep, Two-tone or Morse K. The tone is sent when you release the talk key, just before the carrier drops, so listeners know you are done. Tapping the row plays the new tone on the phone speaker.

topics.title: Transmitting legally
topics.summary: Licences, power and the time limit.

sections.head: Licences
sections.text: You are responsible for the frequencies you use: amateur bands need an amateur licence, GMRS needs a licence in the US, FRS limits power, the licence-free services differ by country (Add a zone marks those your region does not list as "not legal here"; Device → Region), and NOAA weather, marine and railroad channels are receive-only (the app never transmits there). The standard lists in Add a zone say on each one whether a licence is needed.

sections.head: Time limit
sections.text: Device → Longest transmission sets how long one transmission may run: 30 seconds, 1, 2 (the default), 3, 5 or 10 minutes, a custom length (10 seconds or more), or No limit. It applies to everything that transmits: the talk key and the side PTT, the car, the widget, SignalDeck Web, M17, and data such as SSTV, APRS, FT8 and pages. A voice key ends when it reaches the limit (release and key again to continue); data longer than the limit is not sent, and the history says why. The radio's own timer is set a little longer (2 seconds, at most 255 seconds; off for No limit or more than 255 seconds), so SignalDeck always ends the key first. With No limit, or a limit over 255 seconds, the radio does not stop the transmission by itself: only you (release the key) or SignalDeck (its limit or the heat guard) end it, so if SignalDeck were closed or stopped working during a key, the radio would keep transmitting until you end it, for example by restarting the phone. A few modes keep their own shorter limits (the parrot 26 s, voice keyer slots 25 s, pages 25 s, text modes about 26 s per transmission). Choosing more than 2 minutes or No limit shows a heat warning once. Whatever the limit, the heat guard stays on for every key longer than 30 seconds: a voice or M17 key ends at 30 seconds, and long data such as an SSTV picture does not start, while the phone is still cooling down after the last long one (within 1 °C of where it was, or 17 minutes when the temperature cannot be read) or while the radio area is at 60 °C or the battery at 45 °C, and any long key ends early when the radio area passes 70 °C, the battery 48 °C, or either climbs 2 °C in ten seconds. The history says which. In Restricted mode the setting is locked.
